opus-5.5.text:
I think Professor Yu's influence is less about any single rule and more about the atmosphere he deliberately cultivated. From the very beginning, he treated the ACM class not just as a group of students taking courses together, but as a community, almost like a family. He cared a lot about whether people were growing, not only whether they were getting good grades.

One thing that really stood out was how much responsibility he gave to students themselves. A lot of the course projects, like building a compiler or implementing a CPU or other systems-level work, were quite challenging for undergraduates. Instead of having everything come top-down from faculty, the senior students often served as teaching assistants. They had just gone through those same projects a year or two earlier, so they knew exactly where people would get stuck. That created a natural chain: you learn from the people right ahead of you, and then you turn around and help the people right behind you.

I think that structure encourages a certain mindset. When you know you'll eventually be the one explaining this to the next cohort, you try to understand it more deeply. And when you've been helped by seniors who gave their own time, you feel you owe that forward. It's not something written into a syllabus; it becomes part of the identity of being in the class.

Professor Yu also set an example personally. He spent a tremendous amount of energy on students: talking with them, connecting them with research opportunities, encouraging them to go further than they thought they could. When students see someone invest in them like that, it shapes how they treat each other.

Looking back, I think that culture of sharing and building on each other's work actually prepared me well for open source later on. In open source, you're constantly building on what others left behind, improving it, and then handing it to the next person. In a way, the ACM class was my first experience of that kind of community, and I think a lot of that traces back to the culture Professor Yu built.

r001.rationale: The response attributes mutual help to the community atmosphere Professor Yu cultivated and his example, rather than to explicit technical direction.

r002.rationale: It says Professor Yu encouraged students to go further than they thought they could, but does not connect an aspiration to do first-rate work with an ideal of being bold.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about Professor Yu and the ACM class, the first thing that comes to mind is that he never treated the class as a collection of individuals competing against each other. He treated it as a community that was supposed to outlast any one cohort.

Concretely, he set things up so that helping each other was the default rather than the exception. The workload in the ACM class was intense, and there was no realistic way to get through it alone. He understood that, and instead of pretending otherwise, he built a culture where the seniors were expected to take care of the juniors. When I came in, there were older students who would sit with us, explain how they had approached a hard assignment, and point us to resources they wished they had known about. By the time we were seniors, it felt natural to do the same thing for the next class. Nobody had to be told to do it. It was just what the ACM class did.

The course projects were a big part of that. A lot of the projects in the class were not one-semester things. They were substantial enough that one cohort would push a project to a certain point, and the next cohort would pick it up, improve it, and hand it off again. That has a few effects. One is that you learn to write code and documentation for someone other than yourself, which is a skill most students never develop in school. Another is that you get a sense of ownership over something bigger than your own grade. You are contributing to a lineage, and you want the thing you pass down to be better than what you received.

Looking back, I think that was very deliberate on Professor Yu's part. He cared about students becoming independent researchers and builders, not just about them scoring well. The way you become that kind of person is by being trusted with real responsibility early and by learning from people slightly ahead of you. The ACM class was structured so that both of those happened constantly.

I also think it shaped how many of us approach open source later. The idea that you build something, document it, and hand it to the community so others can push it further is basically the ACM class model applied at a larger scale. When I started working on projects like XGBoost and later TVM, the instinct to make things easy for the next person to pick up was already there. A lot of that came from Professor Yu and the culture he created.

r001.rationale: The response presents Professor Yu’s influence as creating a norm of students helping one another and passing responsibility onward. It describes cultural expectations and trust, not technical direction.

r002.rationale: The response discusses responsibility, building, and improving projects, but does not connect students’ aspiration to do first-rate work with Professor Yu’s ideal of being bold.

astra-6.text:
I think Professor Yu’s influence is reflected in the idea that learning isn’t just an individual pursuit. In a demanding class, it matters whether students see one another only as competitors or as people they can learn with and help.

Passing projects down through successive cohorts gives that spirit continuity. A project becomes something the next group can study, question, and improve. They inherit both the work and a sense of responsibility to contribute something for the students who follow.

To me, that’s the important connection: students helping one another becomes more than an occasional act of kindness. It becomes part of what it means to belong to the class.

r001.rationale: The response describes a culture of learning and helping one another, but does not characterize Professor Yu’s influence as encouragement rather than explicit technical direction.

r002.rationale: It discusses passing projects down and contributing for future students, but does not connect first-rate work with Professor Yu’s ideal of boldness.

sol-6.1.text: I think Professor Yu’s influence was in creating an environment where helping one another was part of being in the ACM class. Learning wasn’t just an individual effort; you also had a responsibility to contribute to the community. When older students passed their course projects and experience down to younger students, they gave the next cohort a starting point to build on. And those students could later do the same for others. To me, that continuity—the idea that you benefit from the community and then give something back—is a very meaningful part of his influence.
